answers.headline: No. Even an assault without injury is a crime in Ireland; causing harm carries up to 10 years.
answers.summary: Intentionally or recklessly applying force to someone, or making them believe force is about to be used, without their consent, is assault. Ordinary everyday contact that isn’t meant to hurt doesn’t count. Assault causing harm is a separate, more serious offence.
answers.penalties: Assault: up to 6 months in prison and/or a fine. Assault causing harm: up to 10 years.

answers.headline: No. Corruptly offering anyone, including a Garda, a gift or advantage is a crime.
answers.summary: Corruptly offering or giving a gift, consideration or advantage to anyone as an inducement or reward for doing something in their job is the offence of active corruption.
answers.penalties: Up to 10 years in prison, a fine, and forfeiture of the bribe.

answers.headline: No. Buying or keeping goods you know, or suspect, are stolen is a crime.
answers.summary: Handling stolen property covers receiving or helping dispose of goods knowing they were stolen, or being reckless about it. Simply possessing stolen goods with that knowledge is also an offence. Buying well below market value can be taken as evidence you knew or were reckless.
answers.penalties: Handling: up to 10 years. Possession: up to 5 years.

answers.headline: No. Carrying any knife or bladed article in public is an offence in Ireland, unless you have a good reason.
answers.summary: Having any knife or sharply pointed article in a public place is an offence. It’s a defence to prove a good reason or lawful authority, such as using it for work or a recreational purpose. Flick-knives are treated more strictly.
conditions: Allowed only with a good reason, e.g. work or a hobby
answers.penalties: Up to 12 months and/or €5,000 in the District Court; up to 5 years on indictment.

answers.headline: No. The limit is 50 mg per 100 ml of blood, or 20 mg for learners, new and professional drivers.
answers.summary: Drivers may not drive with more than 50 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood. The limit is 20 mg for ‘specified persons’: learner drivers, drivers in the first two years of their first licence, and drivers of trucks, buses and taxis.
conditions: Learner, novice (first 2 years) and professional drivers: 20 mg/100 ml
answers.penalties: Fines and a driving ban, rising with the alcohol level; prison for higher levels.

answers.headline: No. Murder carries a mandatory life sentence in Ireland.
answers.summary: Anyone convicted of murder must be sentenced to life imprisonment; the judge has no choice. Self-defence can be lawful in narrow circumstances.

answers.headline: No. Possessing cannabis is a crime, though first and second offences for personal use carry only a fine.
answers.summary: Possessing any controlled drug, including cannabis, is an offence. If the court accepts it was for personal use, the first and second offences are punished with a fine only; prison becomes possible from the third offence.
answers.penalties: Personal use: a fine for first and second offences; from the third, up to 12 months (summary) or more on indictment.

answers.summary: Intercepting a call is a crime, but the law’s definition of interception excludes listening or recording where either the caller or the person called has consented. So recording your own call isn’t interception. Data protection rules can still apply, especially for businesses.
conditions: You, or the other side, must consent

answers.summary: It’s an offence to hold a mobile phone while driving a vehicle or a powered personal transporter such as an e-scooter in a public place. Hands-free use isn’t covered by this offence, but you must still drive safely.
answers.penalties: Holding a phone while driving: a fixed fine and penalty points.
